Four moves, every week

ORIENTATION
How we use AI
AI · declared roles

ORIENTATION · AI IN A DECLARED ROLE

AI is a partner you out-think — never a substitute for
thinking.

THE RULE

Always a declared role

Each week AI has one job — this week and next, a 
research assistant that gathers and organises. The role
changes as the term hardens: later it will argue against
you, map rights, scout enforcement. In the final session it
is barred from the room entirely, with one declared role
left in preparation only.

THE HABIT

Ask AI, then disagree

Every week from Week 2 you write a short paragraph, by
hand (150–200 words): what AI said, and where you push
back — where it was wrong, thin, or overconfident. The
judgement stays yours, and the paragraph is individually
assessed.

WHY THE RULES ARE STRICT
Not because the tool is forbidden — because undeclared use teaches you nothing and declared use teaches you
everything. The course's bet is that after ten weeks of using AI in its lane and disagreeing with it in writing, you can out-think
it. The capstone tests exactly that.

Testable: AI always operates in one declared role per week, beginning as research assistant; the weekly "Ask AI, then disagree" paragraph
is handwritten, 150–200 words, individually assessed, and runs from Week 2; at the Week 10 capstone AI is prohibited in the room.

ORIENTATION
What a case week looks like
AI OFF

ORIENTATION · THE PROMISE

From next week, your board gets a file.

THE DOSSIER

Your company's own dispute

A file about your company: how the fight started, where things
stand, and what people are saying — told by partisan voices,
never a neutral narrator. Nobody in the file is objective. Reading
past that is your job.

THE CONTRACT FILE

Two clauses, read word by word

Every dossier carries two verbatim contract extracts. One of
them is the clause the fight is actually about. The other is a trap
— plausible, professional, and not the point. Telling them apart
takes reading, not guessing.

THE QUESTIONS

Withheld until the laptops close

You research with AI in its declared role — but the questions you
must answer arrive on paper only after devices are away. What
you did not genuinely understand, you cannot answer.

THE MORNING TWIST

Something happens on the day

Each case carries a development printed only on the questions
page — new that morning, impossible to prepare for. Your
analysis has to survive it live.

WHY IT IS BUILT THIS WAY
Every mechanism above exists for one reason: so that the work AI can do for you is never the work that is marked. The
tool can gather; it cannot read your file closely, sit in your board's chair, or defend a judgement out loud. That part was
always going to be you.

Testable: a case week's dossier is told by partisan voices with no neutral narrator; it carries two verbatim contract extracts of which one is a
decoy; the questions are withheld until devices are away; and a morning development, printed only on the questions page, must be
answered live.

DIAGNOSTIC
Three questions underneath
AI OFF

DIAGNOSTIC · WHAT THE DILEMMA IS REALLY ASKING

One decision, three questions that run the whole
course.

Sources of law

Where does the rule that "permits" this
even come from? Law is not weather —
every rule has an origin: a statute
passed by a legislature, a constitution
above it, a regulator's standard, a
court's decision, or long custom.
Naming the source is the first step in
knowing how solid a rule is, and who
could change it.

Legal systems

Why is the same discharge legal in one
country and banned in another?
Because countries answer the same
question through different legal
machinery — and a company operating
across borders cannot simply pick the
answer it prefers. Week 2 installs the
two great traditions behind this
disagreement.

Law & morality

Is "legal" the same as "right"? A valid
law tells you what you may do; it has
never fully answered what you should.
The gap between the two is where every
hard decision in this course lives — and
where Northwind's board is standing
now.

KEEP THE THREE APART
"Where does the rule come from?", "whose rule applies?", and "is the rule enough?" are three different questions. Most bad
arguments about Northwind come from answering one while believing you have answered another.

Testable: the three foundation questions are sources of law (every rule has an identifiable origin — statute, constitution, regulation, case
law, custom), legal systems (different countries lawfully answer the same question differently), and law versus morality (a law can be valid
and still not settle what one should do).

BLOCK D
The four questions on every brief

BLOCK D · EVERY SEAT ANSWERS THE SAME FOUR

Different chairs, identical questions. That is what
makes the answers comparable.

1 · Read it from your seat

What does this decision look like from where you sit? What do
you know that the others do not — and what can you not see
from your chair?

2 · Legal versus right

From your seat: is "it's legal" the end of the matter? Say
precisely what the law settles for you — and what it leaves
open.

3 · Whose rule

The host country permits; the home country forbids. Which rule
should govern a company that lives in both worlds — and why
yours?

4 · Commit — and price it

Say what Northwind should do. No fence-sitting. Then say,
honestly, what your choice costs and who pays it — every
option here has a bill.

segments.en: WEEK 1 · WHERE WE STARTED
segments.zh: 第一周·我们从哪里开始

segments.en: Today, "legal" and "right" came apart in your hands, and you argued Northwind's decision from six chairs that were not yours. That is the whole course in miniature: see clearly, weigh honestly, argue every side, then choose — and know the difference between what the law allows and what you owe.
segments.zh: 今天，“合法”和“正确”在你手中分开，你坐在不属于你的六把椅子上争论罗斯文的决定。这就是整个过程的缩影：看清楚，诚实权衡，争论每一方，然后选择——并了解法律允许的和你应该承担的之间的区别。

segments.en: The law told Northwind what it could do. It could not tell Northwind what it should.
segments.zh: 法律告诉罗斯风它能做什么。它无法告诉Northwind它应该做什么。

segments.en: CARRY IT Next week: you saw that countries disagree about the same act. Why? Because the world runs on two great legal traditions — civil law and common law — and Week 2 installs the difference that explains almost everything that follows. Come with your company chosen. The four- block rhythm begins, and the first "Ask AI, then disagree" paragraph is due.
segments.zh: 进行下去 下周：您会看到各国对同一行为存在分歧。为什么？因为世界以两种伟大的法律传统为基础——民法和普通法——而第二周的差异几乎解释了接下来的一切。与您选择的公司一起来。四块节奏开始，第一个“问人工智能，然后不同意”段落即将到来。
segments.explain: 这里的 common law（普通法系）指：判例在法律推理中具有重要地位的法律传统。
